newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin renames communist holiday as Day of Accord.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin renames communist holiday as Day of Accord.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin on Thursday changed the name of a key date in the communist calendar and said the anniversary of the revolution which brought communists to power should be renamed the Day of Accord and Reconciliation.

A decree issued from Yeltsin's hospital ward said November 7 -- now popularly known as Revolution Day -- should remain a national holiday. The Russian president, 65, is recovering from open heart surgery in Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre.
"The revolution of 1917 dramatically changed the destiny of our country," Yeltsin said in the decree.
"Keen not to allow confrontation in the future, in the interests of unity...I declare the November 7 holiday to be the Day of Accord and Reconciliation."
The decree also said 1997 would be named the Year of Accord and Reconciliation.
The changes were likely to please neither Russia's hard-core communists, who were holding rallies across Russia on Thursday to mark the anniversary, nor its radical liberals.
The liberals want the Kremlin to brand the 1917 revolution, the civil war and bloody purges which followed it as crimes against the nation and to denounce communism as a totalitarian ideology.
Radical communists call Yeltsin's administration a "government of occupation" and say there can be no peace between them and the Kremlin unless communism is restored in Russia.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the decree was in line with the new policy of Yeltsin, who played a key role in ending nearly 65 years of communist rule in the former Soviet Union.
"The idea of accord and reconciliation is central to the president's second term," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.

"The president is closing the era of discord and public cataclysm which ravished the country for long years between 1905 and 1993. This is a step by a powerful president," he said, referring to the period between the first democratic revolution and an abortive hardline revolt against Yeltsin.

He said Yeltsin, re-elected in July for a new four-year term in the Kremlin, had set up a commission to prepare events and monuments to commemorate the Year of Accord, which will coincide with the 80th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.
November 7 was the key national holiday in the Soviet Union, marked by parades, concerts and festivals and the traditional military march-past across Red Square before the Politburo.

It was kept on the list of official holidays after the collapse of the Soviet Union, though the government preferred not to dwell on its official title - The Anniversary of the Great October Socialist Revolution.
